Bha li ba li sha he. May these supreme merits bring blessings upon the Emperor for ten thousand myriad years.
O Sage and Enlightened Sovereign, may you occupy the position of the sovereign to whom all nations come to pay homage. Namo Amitāyus.
May the Emperor live for ten thousand myriad years (recite a second time).
By the merit of this sutra and its dhāraṇī, I dedicate it to the Dharma-protecting dragons,
devas, and spirits of the three realms, mountains, and rivers; may these true masters protect the site of practice,
bestowing blessings for peace, security, and well-being, and adorning unsurpassed bodhi.
I universally pray that all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm May together enter the ocean of the nature of Vairocana.
As the incense is first lit, the entire Dharma-realm is perfumed; The ocean-assemblies of all Buddhas smell it from afar, And auspicious clouds form in every place.
As our sincere intention grows ever more earnest, all Buddhas manifest their entire bodies.
Incense-cloud canopies! Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas! (Recite three times) Samantabhadra-rāja Bodhisattva!
May you grace us with your presence upon your elephant-mounted chariot.
There was a bodhisattva sitting in the full lotus posture, named Samantabhadra.
His body was the color of white jade, and he had fifty kinds of light.
These lights, in fifty kinds of colors, formed a halo around his neck. From all the pores of his body, golden light flowed forth.
Upon that golden light-tuft are immeasurable transformation Buddhas, with various transformed Bodhisattvas as their retinue;
they walk slowly and steadily, raining down great precious flowers before the practitioner. That elephant opens its mouth, and upon its tusks—
The jade maidens of the various ponds play drums and music and sing with stringed instruments;
their voices are subtle and wondrous as they praise the Mahāyāna, the Way of Single Reality.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner rejoices and pays homage, further reciting and chanting the most profound sūtras.
I prostrate universally to the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions;
I prostrate to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna and to Śākyamuni, and I also prostrate to Samantabhadra and all the great Bodhisattvas.
I make this vow: if, by virtue of my past merit, I am destined to behold Samantabhadra, [may it be so].
I pray that the Venerable Samantabhadra,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Worthy King, may manifest his form-body for me. (Chanted three times) With all reverence.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddhas who eternally abide throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Dharma that eternally abides throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Sangha that eternally abides throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
These various assemblies each knelt on their right knees and, holding fragrant flowers, made offerings according to the Dharma.
May these fragrant flowers pervade the ten directions, Becoming subtle and wondrous platforms of radiant light;
May the celestial music and divine precious incense, The celestial delicacies and divine precious robes [likewise be offered].
Inconceivable particles of the wondrous Dharma— From each and every particle emerge all particles;

From each and every particle emerge all dharmas. Whirling without obstruction, they mutually adorn one another, Reaching everywhere before the Triple Gem in the ten directions, Before the Triple Gem throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
In every instance, my own body performs offerings, Each and every one pervading the entire Dharma-realm,
Without confusion or obstruction among them, Performing the work of Buddhas throughout the bounds of the future,
Universally perfuming all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm; Upon being perfumed, they all give rise to the Bodhi-mind.
May we together enter the unborn and realize the Buddha-wisdom;
may these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas,
the Honored Dharma, and the Bodhisattvas, as well as the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, and all devas and ṛṣis.
By arising from the Radiant Terrace, Transcending boundless realms, Performing Buddha-works within infinite Buddha-lands,
Universally perfuming all sentient beings, Causing them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta—
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnakusuma (Recite three times).
Śākyamuni Tathāgata, bear witness to this rite of repentance through praise (the recitation of the liturgy with sincerity as is customary).
[The presiding master leads the assembly in chanting praises in the *brahmasvara* voice.
By means of these merits from praising the Triple Gem and the roots of goodness cultivated through the practice of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, we offer this blessing to those in the higher realms.
The eight classes of devas and nāgas; Brahmā King and Śakra Devendra; the four world-protecting kings; the Heaven of the Thirty-three; Yama and the five paths of rebirth;

the six fast days and the eight kings; the spirits who perform beneficial deeds; the celestial physician messengers; and the stars and constellations that protect the Dharma, each together with their retinues.
Within the saṃghārāma, those who protect the True Dharma offer prayers for the longevity of the present Emperor, that he may govern for ten thousand years;

for the Prince, that he may live for a thousand autumns; and for the imperial lineage of golden branches and jade leaves, the governors and ministers of the provinces and districts, the officials and citizens of the realm, and the teachers, monks, parents, and all others.

May the roots of goodness from virtuous and non-virtuous associates, from those who donate to monasteries, and from the faithful offerings of the ten directions—extensively reaching all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm—be used by all to cultivate equally through these roots of goodness.
May they be adorned with all manner of merit and wisdom in this life and in future births.
Together we ascend to the ground of bliss.
(Recite the verse in praise of the Buddha:
The Buddha’s wisdom is the pure moon of suchness; Without conditions, its tranquil illumination shines brightly through the void.
The point where this mind is exhausted is Bodhi; therefore, with a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage.
Now, I shall take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Homage to the past Buddha Vipaśyin. Homage to the Buddha Śikhin.
Homage to Vipaśyin Buddha; homage to Śikhin Buddha; homage to Viśvabhū Buddha;
homage to Krakucchanda Buddha; homage to Kanakamuni Buddha; homage to Kāśyapa Buddha;
homage to our Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha; homage to the Honored Maitreya Buddha of the future.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha!
The unsurpassed, most profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma Is difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
Now that I have seen, heard, received, and upheld it, I pray that you will explain the true meaning of the Tathāgata.

This *Cizhi Dizang Pusa Chanfa* (The Compassionate Repentance Method of Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha) was established so that all sentient beings may give rise to a heart of joy and achieve the benefit of wholesome dharmas;
it is a repentance method undertaken for this purpose. It is intended so that all sentient beings may shatter their afflictions and achieve the benefit of remedial counteraction;
thus one perceives the repentance method. Furthermore, it causes all sentient beings to proceed from precept, concentration, and wisdom through their own hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
One cultivates and perfects the five faculties and powers to attain the benefit of generating wholesome roots, and thus practices the method of repentance.

Furthermore, one causes all sentient beings to cultivate mundane and supramundane deeds and realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), practicing the method of repentance for the sake of these eight kinds of rational benefits.

This is because all sentient beings within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), failing to know as it truly is that the true suchness (*tathatā*) is a single reality, do not abide in true permanence and instead undergo constant fluctuation.

Karma manifests; deluded ignorance arises, taking objective realms as its conditions. The awakened mind, which is inherently still and tranquil, turns away from the Dharma-nature and enters into continuous pervasive conceptualization.

Grasping at self and other, they become causes for one another, resulting in the retributions of good and evil, the three natures including the indeterminate, and the alternating performance of suffering and joy—just as an echo follows a sound or a shadow follows a form in a mirror.
Thus, the common multitude comes into being, giving rise to various marks and undergoing cycles of ascent and descent.

They revolve in succession; bound by fetters, they find it difficult to escape. The *dharmatā* is originally luminous, yet therein they sink and drown. Thus it is said: "The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness.

To awaken to the wondrous principle of "mind-only," both sin and merit are equally empty flowers. To be deluded regarding the perfect luminosity of the *dharmatā*, both good and evil become nothing other than substantial fruits.
Consequently, one transmigrates through the three realms of existence, distancing oneself from the mountain of *nirvāṇa* and swirling in its eddies.
Regarding the four modes of birth, beings enter the ocean of saṃsāra; they create karma wave upon wave and commit transgressions most perilously.

Defilements accumulate like mountains, easily obstructing true emptiness; delusions are as hard as ice, making it difficult to distinguish conventional truth. Moved by these conditions, our Buddha responded by entering the Sahā world.

The World-Honored One Kṣitigarbha arrived in great assembly like gathering clouds; his manifestations appeared like the moon’s reflection in water, and his traces descended like stars scattered across the sky. He exercised the compassion of the same essence...
To deliver sentient beings from the sea of suffering, you manifest the compassion of the unconditioned;

to ferry those in the six realms across the river of craving, you sweep away worldly attachments and cleanse the defilements of delusion. By these causes and conditions, this confession is hereby initiated.

Alas, we [the practitioners] have allowed our minds to be deluded by false objects and our consciousness to be obscured by illusory conditions. Since beginningless kalpas, our retributions have entered this Sahā world, following karma driven by ignorance.

Foolish in distinguishing between the ultimate and the conventional, and biased in their intimacy toward them, they possess discernment yet violate benevolence. Who can distinguish between the worthy and the base, or the acceptable and the unacceptable? Indulging in wine, they are mired in confusion and perpetually lack wisdom;
surrendering to desire, they ruin their moral standards and are constantly possessed by folly. Relying on their own cleverness, they insult others and treat all things with arrogance;
adhering to views derived from others, they remain personally burdened by their own faults and defects. Their transgressions and evils are inexhaustible, and the retribution they attract—
The years have passed without end. If one does not purify the body and mind through repentance, one’s transgressions will surely become as vast as the universe.
When calculating the resulting karmic retribution, one is certain to enter the three miserable realms; until the end of the future, by what means could one attain liberation?

Therefore, we [the undersigned] today lead all those of pure faith, extensively preparing incense and flowers and universally arranging offerings. We establish the ritual altar of the water-moon and perform the *sāṃmārṣṭi* (confession and purification).
I perform this Dharma service to seek compassion and repent for my transgressions. I openly confess and lay bare all offenses already committed, hoping they may be entirely extinguished;
as for faults yet uncommitted, I dare not create them again. Therefore:
I take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.
(One prostration) I take refuge in all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.
(One prostration) I take refuge in all Noble Saṅghas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space. (One prostration)

Next, once again with sincere devotion, we take refuge and pay homage; we entreat Brahmā, Śakra, the Four World-Protecting Kings, the Eight Classes of Devas and Nāgas, and the King of the Netherworld who oversees the paths of karma, to manifest before us and bear witness to our repentance. Therefore, each of us [should] maintain sincere resolve.
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, like the collapse of Mount Tai, I take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas.
Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha;
Namo to Amitābha Buddha; Namo to Maitreya, the Honored Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Lion’s Vigorous Display Endowed with Myriad Practices.
Homage to the Buddha King of the Samādhi of Enlightenment-Flower Sovereignty. Homage to the Buddha Accomplishment of All-Knowledge.
Homage to the Buddha Pure Lotus-Eye. Homage to the Buddha Kāṣāya Banner.
Homage to the Buddha Siṃhanādavikrāntabalendra-rāja.
Homage to the Buddha Guṇamegha. Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadrapraṇidhānarāja. Homage to the Bodhisattva Vasumukha.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Ajita; homage to the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin;
homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; homage to our tutelary deity, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, we next perform repentance: from beginningless time until this very day, we—[the practitioners]—have all...

Because we do not believe that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are the Lords to whom we take refuge; because we do not believe that the wondrous Dharma of the five periods is the food of ambrosia;

and because we do not believe that the sages of the six harmonies are the teachers who guide the deluded, we wander through the three realms in accordance with our delusive habits, cycling through the four modes of birth against the current of saṃsāra, sinking into the sea of suffering with no prospect of liberation. Yet we—

Although they have a rough understanding of the Triple Gem, they have never yet resolved their minds to practice. Furthermore, they harbor notions of "I" and "mine" within, while externally they pursue delusive conditions;
driven by the roots of the three poisons and following the objects of the six sense-fields, they universally commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.

They have extensively promoted killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception; even to the point of widely opening eighty-four thousand gates of the prisons of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and obstructing and closing off eighty-four thousand paths of Prajñā.
The three wholesome paths have been severed, while the four evil paths have been opened. This has continued from beginningless time until now.

They still remain among the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One and the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha gathered at the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, deeply giving rise to compassion and pity, and bestowing grace to repay their fundamental debt.

They taught the practice of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*). Now, regarding the discussion of repentance, one must first repent for the three poisons (*triviṣa*) and the five heinous offenses (*pañcānantarya*).

Once these primary causes are eliminated, karma will have no basis to arise; thus, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala-karma-patha*) will have no way to be committed. As for the dust...
The gates of toil are closed; wondrous practice now lies before us. As the supreme realm communicates in profound stillness, Bodhi may be attained.
Therefore, we [name] and others today give rise to the superior mind (*adhimukti-citta*) and establish firm conduct as the means for extinguishing transgressions.

Then the three poisons, the six sense faculties, and all dependently arisen phenomena will naturally vanish and be forgotten in accordance with our thoughts. Our cultivation of practice shall become sovereign. For this reason, today we seek your compassion.
Confession. Now, one who performs confession should know that afflictions and karma each have their own origins that cause me to wander in saṃsāra;
the three poisons are the fault. Therefore, one first confesses the causes of the afflictions—the three poisons—and subsequently repents for the evil karma and its bitter fruits. Why is this so?
Suffering arises from karma; karma is produced by delusion. Thus, the chain of arising continues without ceasing throughout the three periods of time.

The fundamental cause of this arising ultimately traces back to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). Because the mind gives rise to delusions, the actions of body and speech follow accordingly. Furthermore, this mental karma has three names.
The first is called stinginess and greed; the second is named anger and resentment; the third is doubt and delusion. Because of doubt and delusion, the fetters and afflictions suddenly arise.
Thus we know that the hundreds of thousands of afflictions all have their roots in the three poisons, which cause sentient beings to dwell perpetually within the three miserable realms.
That there are these three realms is entirely due to the nourishment provided by the three poisons, which brings about rebirth in the cycle of birth and death. Even if sentient beings were to...

Having escaped from the hells, they may return to the human realm; yet they again receive a body that is poor, destitute, and exposed, as retribution for their past stinginess, greed, and lack of faith in the Buddha.

If there are sentient beings who, having completed their retribution in the realm of hungry ghosts, return to the ranks of humanity, they again receive a body that is fierce, perverse, stubborn, and dull-witted, as the karmic reward for not believing in the Mahāyāna. If there are sentient beings who escape the path of animals and are born...
Within the human relations, they are foolish and devoid of wisdom, like those intoxicated or deluded, because they failed to follow the community in their cultivation and study.

Due to these causes and conditions, the three paths are transmitted through the postal relay; though the retributions they receive differ in a thousand ways, if one examines their original source, each proceeds from the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Since the karma of the mind already brings such bitter retribution, how can one remain at ease without repentance? However...
These three types are all called "poisons" because they can extinguish the wisdom-life of the *dharmakāya* of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, these afflictions are called "ignorance and delusion" (*avidyā-sammoha*) because they can disturb and confuse sentient beings with turbid and vexing phenomena.
Moreover, these afflictions are called "defiled ignorance" (*kliṣṭa-ajñāna*) because they can shroud the purity of the *tathatā* within the aggregates.
For this reason, these afflictions are also called "enemies and bandits," because they can destroy the fivefold Dharma-body of sentient beings and their wealth of meritorious qualities.

They are also called the "river of craving," because they sweep sentient beings away into the ocean of birth and death, preventing them from reaching the shore of Nirvana. They are also called "prisons," because they can bind...

Because they shackled sentient beings, preventing them from attaining liberation and sovereignty. Thus, these afflictions (*kleśa*) drag one through the six realms of existence and bind one to the four modes of birth.
They cause the creation of boundless karma and ensure that the cycle of rebirth never ceases; all of this is due to these afflictions acting as the intermediaries for thieves.

They marry one to a thousand varieties of calamity and wed one to ten thousand distinct forms of suffering. Therefore, we [the practitioners] today, with sincere resolve, seek compassion and repent. As...

These are the three poisons; one should contemplate them and eliminate them. Furthermore, contemplate that for [Name] and others, from beginningless time until now, although they have received retribution in human form and have practiced wholesome dharmas, they remain bound by:
first, cessation; second, contemplation; third, causes; fourth, conditions; fifth, the five aggregates; sixth, the six obscurations; seventh, the seven destinies; eighth, the eight inversions;
ninth, existence; tenth, objects; eleventh, the pervasive proclivities; and twelfth, the sixteen heavy cities. One should know these.
The eighteen realms, the twenty secondary views, the twenty-five notions of self, the sixty-two views, the eighty-eight afflictions of view, the ninety-one afflictions of cultivation,
the one hundred and eight branches of secondary defilements, and the eighty-four thousand afflictions— each according to its original number—
are all tied to ignorance. Day and night they blaze fiercely, pressing forward upon the waves of consciousness and constricting the source of the mind, thereby opening the gates of the outflows.

The ocean surges and submerges True Suchness (*tathatā*), vexing and disturbing the sages and worthies. The six realms and four modes of birth are deluded regarding the three voids (*trishūnya*), and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are obscured.
Such afflictions (*kleśa*) completely cover enlightened clarity; as karmic retribution takes hold of the mind, the body finds it difficult to escape.

Therefore, today I entreat the Compassionate Honored One with deep sorrow: please accept my earnest and sincere repentance. May the knots and habitual tendencies of affliction melt away in a single thought.

Pure. Having perfected the practice and realization of the tasks of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, I look up with aspiration to the Triple Gem of the ten directions, the Ten Wheels, Kṣitigarbha, and the Benevolent One (Avalokiteśvara).
By the power of your original compassion, the power of your original mercy, and the power of your vows and spiritual transformations, please accept us.

Through our earnest supplication and full confession, may all afflictions be entirely subdued and severed; may our practices and vows become brilliant and clear, and may the fruit of Bodhi ripen. One.
The causes for all births are forever and never again to be experienced. With mutual resolve and faith, they shared an equal and piercing sense of urgency.
Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground like a great mountain collapsing, they reverently directed their thoughts toward the ten directions and paid homage to all Buddhas.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, one next performs repentance (*pratikramana*). Now, as for repentance, it refers to reforming the past and cultivating the future, so as to repent for what was formerly done and renew oneself.

While present karma is easy to restrain and spiritual practice can be mastered, habitual tendencies from past lives are difficult to eliminate; these must necessarily rely upon the methods of repentance.

Yet, those who practice today prefer the correct while remaining firmly attached to the perverse, and desire purity while being biased toward defilement. They are capable of this without instruction and do not even wish for it.
Yet it happens spontaneously; if there is something that seems to drive one on and cannot be stopped, this is what past habits impel.

When virtue is lofty yet conduct is base, or when one performs good deeds yet the person suffers misfortune—abounding in obstacles and deficiencies, frequently plagued by illness and vexation, stretching on as if bound by a mechanism that cannot be released—this is what accumulated karma summons. This is not the result of a single lifetime...
The conditions for the kalpa have been such that, from time immemorial, seeds have been perfumed moment by moment, ripening into fruition, and manifesting as active formations;

thus, it cannot be resolved except through repentance. Yet, if one wishes to repent for past transgressions, one must rely on future practice and conduct to achieve entry into the state of sainthood and transcendence of the mundane—all of which proceeds from this undertaking. One should follow the Buddha’s words and act according to the Dharma.

In practicing cultivation, one must first know where to rest. With a rectified mind and sincere intention, one’s virtue will shine forth. When one knows where to rest, the mind becomes settled and tranquil; thus, no evils are committed.
When the mind is rectified and anxieties are stilled, all manner of goodness will surely be practiced. When sincerity moves things, past transgressions are transformed.
This is especially worthy of clarification. If one’s bright virtue is renewed, then future merit and wisdom may be expected.
Do not doubt that small good deeds bring no blessing; if you do not perform even small good deeds, how can you achieve sainthood? Do not doubt that small evils may be committed with impunity;

if small evils accumulate, they are sufficient to destroy one’s very person. Each of you should strive diligently to together repent of your transgressions. As the Sūtra says: "The nature of sin is fundamentally..."
Emptiness. Because it is falsely constructed by the mind, the substance of merit has no foundation; yet all is obtained from the mind.
Since transgressions are falsely constructed within emptiness, merit likewise seeks its locus within the self-mind. Yet we, [Name] and others, have not yet departed from the stage of ordinary beings;

we are utterly deluded in every encounter, and our actions do not rely upon the sacred scriptures. How can our repentance be deemed sublime? Therefore, today we give rise to a courageous and resolute mind.
One should arouse a mind of diligent effort and repent for past transgressions. Now, the power of the merit of repentance is inconceivable. Why is this?

When the five signs of decline appear in the heavens, one may still restore their celestial status through repentance; when the retribution for patricide or regicide ripens in the human realm, one may return to the human path through remorse.
It can cause the practitioner to attain peace and happiness. If one can exert oneself with sincere devotion and a resolute heart...

By confessing and revealing [one's faults], the causes and conditions of the three obstacles will naturally be extinguished. For this reason, we, [Name] and others, seek refuge and repent with earnest supplication.

Furthermore, from the beginningless cycle of birth and death until now, because of ignorance, the retributive fruits have been inexhaustible; due to the nature of afflictions, [the suffering continues].

They commit the ten unwholesome karmas; they are immersed in and attached to defilement; their greed and desire rush forth; they bind themselves to form and flow with craving; their essential desires are afflictions;

they engage in mutual strife through anger and resentment; harboring malice toward others despite their innocence; their karmic actions of killing are afflictions; and their nature and consciousness are deluded.

Discriminating neither between good and evil, they perceive only form and mind; muddled by afflictions, they cling to "I" and "mine. They treat others with contempt and arrogance toward all things, usurping positions of honor and authority.

Possessing the affliction of overweening pride, they harbor doubts regarding the holy teachings, failing to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, and finding it difficult to determine their proper conduct.
The affliction of doubt and hesitation: they deny cause and effect, clinging to annihilationism or eternalism, and fall forever into the pit of views. The affliction of precepts and rituals:

failing to recognize that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are dependently designated, they cling to the four inversions and remain deluded regarding the three periods of time, bringing harm both to others and to themselves.
They constantly dwell in the three miserable realms; they are bound by the afflictions of extreme views; they associate with evil friends and distance themselves from virtuous people;

they neglect right knowledge and are entangled by the affliction of the view of a self-identity. These twenty secondary afflictions bind them to the three realms, causing them to undergo the four modes of birth throughout the cycle of transmigration.
There is no end to this cycle. Now, we [so-and-so] and others openly confess and beseech your compassion, repenting for all our transgressions.

Furthermore, in accordance with the nature of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), we have lacked shame and dread of blame, feared neither spirits nor deities, and failed to understand cause and effect, thereby committing boundless sins.

They have never repented their transgressions. Furthermore, they are stingy and greedy for their own possessions, begrudging them and refusing to give to others. Upon seeing the wealth and treasures of others, they wrongfully seize and covet them.

Their five senses are extravagant and dissolute; they harbor no thoughts of the six mindfulnesses. They are negligent in body and mind, failing to restrain their afflictions. Their mental conduct is corrupt and evil, and their path deviates from pure regulations.
They act with partiality and cruelty, unable to endure their own afflictions. This is the dharma of indolence and negligence, which is contrary to the principle of reason.

Clever and sharp; drifting and lax; indolent regarding afflictions (*kleśa*); tranquil yet restless; slow and heavy in movement; indulgent and self-willed; failing to exert oneself against afflictions;
giving rise to thoughts upon encountering objects; unable to distinguish right from wrong; agitated and forgetful; ignorant afflictions;
anger, derision, suffering and pleasure, defamation and praise, gain and loss—chasing after these with emotional abandon; the affliction of hypocrisy and confusion; flattery.

Regarding temporal states: these are afflictions of flattery, crookedness, and entanglement; of concealing and hiding one's virtues; and of lack of sincerity. They consist of being easily provoked to anger and difficult to please;

of envying the virtuous; and of flattery, deception, craving, and arrogance. These are afflictions of harmful poison—being right in the face but wrong behind one's back, deviating from the sutras and violating the scriptures, using unrighteous means to sting others, and following one’s own whims while suppressing one’s integrity under the pretext that it is "timely and appropriate.
This extends even to the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, both mundane and supramundane.
In the interim, one contemplates the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination in forward order and their cessation in reverse order.

The wheeling of afflictions extends to as many as the sands of the Ganges, obstructing the path of transformation. Ignorance halts midway, giving rise to the six coarse states and setting in motion the three subtle states;

all this is due to the inherently evil nature of afflictions, which shroud the secret treasury of the mind-ground. Thus, with these causes of delusion, one illusorily fashions the fruits of karma. As it is said:

Today I seek mercy and repent. Relying upon the merit of my current diligence and the supernatural power of all Buddhas, may the ten fetters be forever stilled and the three poisons suddenly forgotten.

May the delusions and afflictions of the three categories be exhausted without remainder; may I be liberated from the three miserable realms within body and mind, never forgetting for even a single thought the ground of wisdom.
May I open the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment and realize the fruit of the ten stages before the Buddha.

Bodhisattvas, having equally attained non-arising and extensively benefited both themselves and others, entered the treasury of the mind-ground. Having completed their repentance and made their vows, they took refuge in and paid homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
Praising the Secret Treasury of the Mind-ground: Ensnared by afflictions, body, speech, and mind become interconnected, creating boundless and vast transgressions.
I prostrate to the Golden Immortal; all evils are simultaneously cleansed.
Namo Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva (Recite three times; proceed with the ritual for the Confession as usual).

the bee-king of Bodhisattvas feeds upon its nectar. I now pay homage to the Buddha-lotus.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, one next proceeds to repentance. Thus far, the brief repentance for the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is complete; the hindrances of delusion are now purified.
Karmic causes do not persist; karma has no counterpart. By what means could one commit offenses? Next, one should repent of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).

Although the manifestations of karma are many—whether outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), black or white—if one examines them, none will remain uncollected. Yet the Buddha spoke of the five precepts, and the Confucians speak of the five constants.

Though the constants and precepts differ, their essence is fundamentally one. To subdue oneself and restore benevolence, and to possess a compassionate heart that does not kill—when one sees [a living being]...

Seeking profit through righteous means; not taking what is not given; not looking upon what is improper; rather than permitting depravity or allowing words to be fickle, one maintains that "trust cuts through metal";

and avoiding the destruction of the self through wine and the ruin of virtue through falsehood, thereby firmly upholding the constant precepts so that the human path remains unimpaired—these five wholesome karmas are likewise termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*), because they cannot transcend the realm of shared existence (*sahā-loka*). Furthermore, there is a superior class [of beings].
Not only was he free from stinginess with his own possessions, but he also used his wealth to benefit others. He did not merely abstain from killing; rather, his very nature delighted in life.

Although he had not yet transcended desire, his conduct was measured and restrained. He praised the ten wholesome paths of action, extolled the protection of the One Vehicle, gathered his scattered mind through diligent effort, and cultivated the *anāgamya-samādhi*.

The resulting retribution causes them to dwell on earth; they preside over a small chiliocosm, and their reward resembles that of superior humans, yet all remain within the realm of outflows (*āsrava*).

Furthermore, there are those who loathe the suffering, coarseness, and impurity of desire and rejoice in the purity and subtlety of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); by practicing the four dhyānas, they attain rebirth among the eighteen classes of heavens.

Although they have suppressed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they have not yet eradicated them; the outflows of form have not been eliminated. Yet again, there are those of profound capacity who loathe the confinement of the form realm and seek to exhaust consciousness and return to...

Emptiness. One contemplates the cessation of the perception of emptiness; because there is no place of abiding, one reaches the Peak of Extinction (*bhavāgra*). There, the lifespan lasts for *saṃkhyeya* kalpas, yet one eventually falls back into saṃsāra.

Having not yet attained the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*), this is also termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). As with humans or devas mentioned above, although they cultivate wholesome karma, they do not transcend saṃsāra;

all such cases are collectively termed "black karma. If one cultivates meditative contemplation, relying on the contemplation of emptiness—beginning from the stage of the five stabilizing minds (*pañca-vasthāpana-citta*)—in total...

Regarding the objects of distinct characteristics—the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—one successively accomplishes the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as the auxiliary path and contemplates the sixteen aspects of the noble truths as the primary cultivation.
One destroys the eighty-eight latent tendencies of the views and realizes the Path of Seeing;

one eliminates the ninety-one latent tendencies of the thought-processes, personally realizes non-arising, and the mind and its objects reach quiescence. Through right universal emptiness, one becomes detached from the five aggregates.
Mountains emerge from the sea of birth and death and dwell upon the summit of nirvana; yet, being unconditioned by the Dharma, they cannot deliver sentient beings and are not yet called Bodhisattvas.

If one, within the vehicle of the Hearers (Śrāvaka-yāna), contemplates the nature of dharmas through dependent origination—from ignorance conditioned by volitional formations, up to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—[one still does not attain true liberation].

From the cessation of ignorance, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction also cease. Thus, by contemplating the nature of phenomena through both the reverse and direct orders, delusions are stilled and wisdom is extinguished;

one swiftly realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Those whose illness lies in a lack of spiritual capacity all attain the minor fruits. As for those called Bodhisattvas, they belong to the Mahāyāna.
Having not yet crossed over oneself, one first delivers sentient beings; initiating the *saṃnāha* (armor) at the very first thought, one proceeds toward hardships with ultimate great compassion.

Extensively practicing the six *pāramitās*, one’s merit transcends the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Cultivating the wisdom-activities of both outflowing and non-outflowing, one attains the compassionate love of the unborn and the non-arising.
Opening the vision and knowledge of the Buddha, one realizes the ultimate self-nature, unifying it with the primordially existing spiritual luminosity, and awakening to the ground of the mind.

The secret treasury—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—all ultimately converge in the three virtues. Yet, the reason we are unable to attain liberation is entirely due to the lack of stability in our fundamental consciousness;
as it pursues external objects, the mind arises, leading to the accumulation of defiled habits and the binding of karma, and the ripening of pure habits into their respective fruits.

Performing good and performing evil, they have never paused for a moment. Circulating through the five realms and traversing the four modes of birth, they pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Bewildered by obstacles and difficulties, they are like fish swimming in a net, about to enter the great current; even if they should briefly escape, they encounter the net once again.
However, due to deluded views, deluded habits arise. One wanders through the three realms like a postal relay and passes through the four modes of birth like a traveler in an inn.
Emerging and submerging without cease, one invites severe retribution for oneself; all this is because of ten kinds of deluded habits, preventing liberation.
What are these ten? First, the habit of lustful intercourse; second, the habit of greedy inhalation; third, the habit of arrogant mutual disparagement; fourth, the habit of anger...

1. The habit of mutual conflict; 2. The habit of mutual hatred; 3. The habit of mutual jealousy; 4. The habit of mutual deception; 5. The habit of mutual seduction through fraud; 6. The habit of mutual slander through deceit;
7. The habit of mutual resentment; 8. The habit of mutual clarity through views; 9. The habit of mutual oppression through injustice; 10. The habit of mutual clamor through litigation.

Due to these ten habits, one creates the ten evil fruits. All arise from the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which construct various [karmas] leading to retribution in the hells. The six sense organs...
They mutually receive [the karmic fruit]. For these reasons, one must perform repentance.
First, regarding the habit of sexual desire: when the male and female organs and their objects meet and rub against one another, this friction does not cease;

it agitates the sense-faculties and their objects. You pity my physical form, and I cherish your mind; as days, months, and years pass, we grow increasingly debilitated and fall into a state of exhaustion. We sleep...
In dreams, one’s body is restless; the limbs ache with pain, and one is filled with sorrow and finds no joy.

As death approaches, parents and wife are distressed, deeply wounded by the separation from the deceased. The consciousness of the departed wanders on day and night; having departed, it cannot be turned back.

One must immediately undergo the retribution of the iron bed, suffering for kalpas—immeasurable and boundless. For this reason, all Buddhas characterize sexual misconduct as being identical [to other grave evils].
This is called the fire of desire. When Bodhisattvas see lust, they avoid it as they would a pit of fire.
Yet from beginningless time until now, both myself and sentient beings have fundamentally failed to know how to distance ourselves from sensual desire and avoid the fiery pit of lust.

Regarding internal and external objects—the physical forms of men and women—we become deluded by form and deluded by mind, extensively creating foul karma, destroying our own pure precepts, violating the prohibitions regarding the nature of others, bringing shame upon their families, and ruining them.

My name is Xianjie. Being neither male nor female, I am one of the five classes of non-humans. Or perhaps as a bhikṣuṇī, I indulged in sensual desires and created the causes for rebirth in hell, suffering immeasurable pain.
Therefore, today, in the respectful presence of the sages and worthies, I lay bare my heart and confess my transgressions with earnest supplication.
I pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the compassionate Maitreya (Dizang) will pour down the water of nectar to wash away the stains of my sins, so that—

My beginningless habituation to desire has been transformed into the pure conditions for śīla; having reached ultimate bodhi and perfected the virtue of precepts, I have ascended to the Stage of Joy and forever severed the cycle of saṃsāra.

Second, regarding the repentance for the habituation of greed: the karma of the habituation of greed manifests as a mutual attraction that arises and continues without ceasing, causing the roots of greed to spread like creeping vines.
It is like a magnet and iron needles of the same kind. One who knows contentment is joyful even in poverty; one who lacks contentment seeks more even in wealth.
Little do they realize that wealth invites ultimate calamity, leading to the ruin of the family, the loss of life, and the dispersal of one's kin.
Separation. Furthermore, there are three conditions by which what is not sought arrives of its own accord: one may encounter water or fire, suffering unexpected and unjust calamities;

or one may give birth to a rebellious child, leading to the neglect of the Dharma and the ruin of the family estate, such that the household wastes away until it is emaciated, with suffering like that of having one's flesh carved out. Even if one can skillfully defend against these, depletion and dissipation will have no end.
For this reason, the Buddhas designate those who seek much as being of the same nature as the "water of greed. When Bodhisattvas see greed, they avoid it as they would [a dangerous place].
The Miasmic Sea. From beginningless time until now, I and all beings have remained entirely ignorant; seeking much, we suffer much, never escaping this miasmic sea.

We recklessly race about in pursuit of heavy and light treasures, profit and status, whether public or private, mutually attracting and seizing through evil means, plundering and looting, and inflicting wanton harm upon the innocent people.
Regarding the wealth of the Triple Gem, we use it in a confused and impure manner, feigning public or private benefit to evade our duties and transgress the law.

At passes and ferries, they steal by the grain of rice or the ounce; they deceive by the inch or the pint. They trade the coarse for the fine, exchange the short for the long, employing a hundred clever stratagems in hopes of gaining a mere hair’s breadth.
This increases their greedy hearts; insatiable in their desire for gain, they undergo the cycle of rebirth.
Therefore, today I earnestly beseech the Buddha to have compassion and accept my repentance. May all karmic deeds of greed be entirely eliminated. By virtue of this—

Through the merit of this ritual repentance, may the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) increase; by means of this supreme cause, may the *pāramitās* be fulfilled, the pure mind be thoroughly attained, and one ascend to the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Third, regarding the repentance for the habit of pride: the habits of pride intersect and assail one another, arising from mutual reliance. They flow on without ceasing, surging and rushing forward;
the ocean of ignorance is vast, and the waters of greed are deep. It is like the mouth and tongue, which produce flavor through their mutual interaction, thereby generating water.
As they strike against one another, they form enmity over successive kalpas, attacking and disputing one another, with their litigation extending even through births and deaths.

There are retributions such as the Blood Lake, the River of Ashes, Hot Sands, and molten copper poured into the mouth; for this reason, all Buddhas designate pride (*māna*) by the same name as the "Ocean of Delusion.

When Bodhisattvas perceive pride, they avoid it as if fleeing from a great drowning. [Name] and the assembly have, from beginningless time until now, remained entirely unaware that we are drowning in the waters of delusion and pride;
tossed by the eight winds of the world, with waves piling up in a thousand folds, we drift through birth and death.
They sink into the ocean of the river of arrogance and views; they hoist the sail of pride and enter the current of ignorance, swimming and drowning in its vast expanse with no prospect of emergence.
Furthermore, some rely on their noble lineage to be arrogant toward others, or use their cleverness to despise and deceive their junior students.

Even before attaining anything, they claim attainment; before realizing anything, they claim realization. They falsely usurp the vessels of the Way and deceitfully mislead later generations. Such are these [people].
Pride cannot be fully described. Facing the Triple Gem with reverence, I repent it all. May I [Name] perfect the dhyāna of tranquility and complete the pāramitā of patience;
may I cross the ocean of pride and delusion, ascend the mountain of nirvāṇa, give rise to the light of wisdom, and enter the stage of the One Vehicle.
Fourth, regarding the repentance for the habit of anger: when the habit of anger clashes, it gives rise to mutual antagonism.

This antagonism binds without ceasing, heating the mind until it ignites like fire, forging one’s vital energy (*prāṇa*) into metal. From this conflict arises evil karma; in life there are wheels of knives, swords, halberds, axes, hatchets, saws, and spears.

These arise from clashing with resentment, and the murderous vapors fly and stir. When the habits of anger strike one another, there are punishments of imprisonment, nose-cutting, decapitation, amputation, and mincing.
The retribution for piercing, striking, and beating is such that all Buddhas designate anger with the same name as "sword.
When a Bodhisattva sees anger, they avoid it as they would an execution. From beginningless time until now, I and the multitude have never realized the evil habit of anger;
we have grasped at these mutual conflicts—teachers angry at disciples, disciples angry at teachers, parents and the six types of kin, and relatives and old friends.
In the past, neighbors and fellow villagers would repeatedly clash with one another, falling into disorderly competition and vowing never to reconcile.

Failing to reflect upon their own lack of wisdom while seeing that others possess the conditions for merit, they vainly disputed over superiority and inferiority, vying with one another to forge enmities.
They sought every means to gloss over their own faults and extensively spread the dust of others' rare transgressions. Thus, their anger and hatred were immeasurable and boundless; therefore—
Now, facing the holy sages with reverence, I repent for all habitual tendencies toward anger. Through the diligent practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, may I perfect the *pāramitās*.
With the blazing wisdom further clarified, may I realize the Unsurpassed Way and widely cause all sentient beings to ascend together to the Fourth Stage.
Fifth, the confession of the habit of deception: Deceptive practices involve mutual enticement, giving rise to agitation and incessant derision that provokes afflictions.
Like water soaking a field where weeds and tares grow, they wither the fine grain so that virtuous seeds do not sprout. Deceptive habits perpetuate one another;
right and wrong are falsely constructed, and through the fabrication of heterodox arguments, one deceives the powerful and suppresses both self and others. I confess this.

Deceiving oneself and others, crookedly flattery according to the times, and using the crooked to oppose the straight, one receives retributions such as handcuffs, fetters, stocks, shackles, canes, whips, clubs, and blows.
For this reason, all Buddhas identify the crafty and the false with the same name: slanderers and thieves.
When Bodhisattvas see deception, they fear it as they would a jackal or a wolf. Yet from beginningless time until now, we have utterly failed to recognize these crafty wolves and slanderers.
Human beings are likewise. They instead pursue their long-standing habits and give rise everywhere to flattery and artifice. They frequent noble households and overturn virtuous families.
Unable to bear loyalty and faithfulness, they are biased, deceitful, and innocent of merit. They incite one another, engaging in neither right action nor right conduct.

Abandoning the Eightfold Noble Path, they seek through wrong livelihoods and wrong pursuits, losing their bodies and forfeiting their lives—all bound by conditions of deception. Through such causes as these, they commit immeasurable sins until the end.
This invites bitter fruits from which there is no means of escape. Therefore, today, facing the Holy Ones and Sages with reverence, I seek compassionate repentance.

I pray that the Triple Gem and the Compassionate Honored One, Kṣitigarbha, will take pity upon me and accept me, bearing witness to my confession. May the five habitual tendencies mentioned above be entirely eliminated;
may I enter the *nāga-samādhi* through the samādhis and dhāraṇīs, and may the perfection of dhyāna be fully realized at every thought. May I exhaustively...

Until the ultimate attainment of Bodhi, may they give rise to unimpeded eloquence and inexhaustible joy in teaching, extensively receiving all sentient beings so that they may cross the ocean of saṃsāra and together ascend to the other shore.
Having passed beyond the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), may they realize the unconditioned state of Buddhahood.
You who are present here, let us together with sincere resolve and equal, piercing earnestness take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha. Homage to Vajradhvaja Buddha.
Homage to Kanakaprabhāsa Buddha. Homage to Suvarṇakuṇḍala Buddha.
Homage to Vīrasena Buddha. Homage to Vīrarata Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnārcis. Homage to the Buddha Ratnacandra.
Homage to the Buddha Abhimukta. Homage to the Buddha Ratnacandra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Siṃhadhvaja. Homage to the Bodhisattva Siṃhakāra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja. Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbharāja.
Having paid homage to all Buddhas, one next performs repentance. Sixth is the habit of deception, wherein mutual accusations and false delusions ceaselessly continue;

the mind practices fraud and commits villainy, resulting in impurities such as excrement, urine, and foul speech. Like dust driven by the wind, each person sees nothing of the other, yet they experience the retributions of suffering—sinking and drowning, leaping and surging, flying and falling, drifting and submerging.
Therefore, the Buddhas characterize this deception as being like [the following]:* *(Note: The original text appears to be incomplete at the end.)*
Bandits! When Bodhisattvas see such deceptions, they tread upon them as if they were venomous snakes.
Yet from time immemorial until this very day, we and the multitude have still not recognized these deceitful serpents and have never distanced ourselves from them.

Following the habit of deception, our minds calculate perverse views, our mouths utter false words: seeing, we say we do not see; hearing, we say we do not hear; knowing, we say we do not know; and doing, we say we do not do.
They do not act with integrity; they are right in the face but wrong behind their backs. They deceive the ignorant and betray both gratitude and righteousness.

They treat those close to them as strangers and preach deceptive, false doctrines to mislead the foolish. Having spoken, they claim to have ascended to the rank of the sages; yet when disparaging others, they fall to the level of commoners.
Yet they do not realize that they have entered the pit of false views and are leading others into hell, thereby inviting immeasurable and boundless retribution of suffering.
If one does not repent, how can this be extinguished? Therefore, today, in reverent presence of the Buddhas, I lay each matter bare and seek compassionate repentance.
From this day forward, I shall practice with sincerity; may wisdom manifest before me, and may I fulfill the *pāramitās*. Truly...
One speaks truthful words; one is neither deceptive nor fraudulent. Through diligence toward Bodhi, one awakens to the treasury of the mind-ground.
Seventh, when the habitual tendencies of resentment intersect with mutual dislike, they give rise to harbored hatred. Preceded by anger, one harbors malice without ceasing;

taking the formation of enmity as its nature, one is unable to exercise forbearance. With feverish distress and frantic agitation, one then resorts to verbal accusations and petitions, litigating before the public courts.

Therefore, flying stones and hurled rocks, boxes stored in carriage frames, jars filled and bags packed—like a person of hidden malice harboring evil within, there are acts of throwing, seizing, striking, stabbing, tossing, and grasping without interval.
For this reason, the Buddhas designate resentment as being identical to a malevolent ghost.
When a Bodhisattva sees an enemy, it is like drinking poisoned wine; so too for myself and all sentient beings.
From beginningless time until now, they have truly not known that their resentment is like poisoned wine;

intoxicated within the house of ignorance, their habitual enmities clash and loathe one another, harboring grudges and feuding, whether toward their parents through acts of defiance and filial impiety, or toward their brothers and sisters.
Toward paternal and maternal aunts, uncles, kinsmen, good friends, and fellow monks with whom I have lived together, I have failed to follow the teachings and lacked proper instruction.

Such resentment and hatred have not yet been expiated through repentance. Therefore, today, facing the Triple Gem and the Compassionate Honored One Kṣitigarbha, may all the enmities I have harbored since birth be completely extinguished.
As for karmic enmities not yet formed, I dare not commit them again. May my wisdom travel far.

One should bring to mind the accomplishment of the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā). Truly realizing its essence, one becomes endowed with spiritual power (ṛddhi-bala) and manifests transformations throughout the ten directions to deliver all those subject to outflows (sāsrava), leading them to the mountain of nirvāṇa.

Eighth, as the views and habitual tendencies interact and clarify one another, they give rise to mutual opposition. When this opposition does not cease, one harbors restrictive precepts and prohibitions;

thus, various false views arise in mutual contradiction. Consequently, there emerge masters, officials, and bureaus who adjudicate words and phrases, investigating and scrutinizing the perverse and the false.
Like travelers on a road meeting one another as they come and go, these habitual tendencies intersect; their retribution involves interrogation, weighing, and measuring.

They deliberate and investigate; they examine with clarity as if looking into a mirror. Admitting and submitting to their verdicts, the judges of good and evil, along with various youths, hold documents and vouchers in their hands to distinguish between rumors and falsehoods, and to interrogate on matters such as these. For this reason, all Buddhas designate them as "wrong views."
It is called the "Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas perceive all manner of delusions, pervasive conceptualization, and pervasive clinging, they regard them as if facing a precipice of poison.
From beginningless time until now, both myself and the multitude have failed to realize that false views manifesting together are like a precipice of poison.

Regarding the principles of the Truths, we engage in false calculations and reckless speculations, grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, giving rise to various false views, and becoming attached to annihilationism, eternalism, or even emptiness.

There exist those who hold to the view of precepts and the view of ascetic practices; they give rise to thoughts according to their circumstances, deny cause and effect, and falsely cite perverse conditions, claiming them to be the true path.

Furthermore, there are those who confuse delusion for clarity, such as throwing themselves off cliffs, plucking out their hair, consuming filth, or lying upon wooden stumps—engaging in these harmful ascetic practices under the mistaken belief that they are meritorious.
Consequently, at the end of their lives, they fall directly into the Avīci Hell. Such views and karmic actions have indeed occurred in the past; therefore, I...
Today, reverently facing the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, I take refuge in the Compassionate Honored One, Kṣitigarbha.

I repent for wrong views and wrong thoughts, and shall henceforth establish right knowledge and right view. (I, [Name], together with the assembly, with upright minds unmoving, ascend to the high Eighth Stage.

May we fulfill the Pāramitās in this very life, and together with all sentient beings, may we all attain the fruits of sainthood and realize the unconditioned, returning together to the ultimate truth.)
The Secret Treasury.
Ninth, regarding the habit of deception: when habits of deception intermingle, they arise from fraud. Because of such deceitful slander, one lacks sincerity within;
yet in praising others for their virtues, one fears only that they may not reach heaven, while in disparaging others for their faults, one especially dreads that they might not fall [into hell].

Yuan [said]: "To revile and destroy the virtuous, to disparage and expel the śramaṇas, to have a will that is not loyal and upright, and a mind that harbors hypocrisy—for these reasons, there are matters such as being pressed by mountains, struck by stones, ground by mills, and crushed under plows.
Just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrong the worthy and good, they habitually engage in mutual exclusion;

thus, there are various events such as being pinned down, squeezed, and forced through narrow passages. For this reason, the Buddhas designate those who harbor resentment and slander as being the same [as such beings]."

He is named the "Slanderous Tiger. When a Bodhisattva encounters such injustice, it is like being struck by a bolt of lightning. From beginningless time until now, I and the multitude have remained unaware that our habitual practice of deception and slander is exactly like that of this Slanderous Tiger.
Whether through the abuse of legal authority to falsely incriminate kin and friends, or through slandering and harming preceptors, monks, and other people, their hearts lack compassion and patience;
they are cruel and merciless toward the innocent—the widowers, the widows, the orphans, and the solitary—inflicting harm upon them without cause.
Luo Qi suffered a calamity that led to his death in grievous injustice, for which it was difficult to seek redress. Such acts of resentment and slander produce boundless karmic consequences.
Therefore, I now, with right intention and sincere heart, reverently face this holy assembly to confess and repent. May all my habits of wrongful conduct be completely dissolved like melting ice.
Through the power of the fulfillment of my vows and the perfection of *pāramitā*, may I never again give rise to evil thoughts or create further karma for the three miserable realms forevermore.
To gather in humans and devas, one should cultivate wise insight to guide sentient beings so that they may together return to perfect enlightenment.
Tenth, regarding the repentance for the habit of litigation: the habit of litigation involves clamorous disputes arising from concealment;

one is unable to hide one's own faults and promote the good, but instead envies the virtuous and resents the capable, proclaiming hidden evils to make others find it difficult to tolerate them, fearing only that one might not prevail.

When one person surpasses another, their spirit becomes arrogant and obstinate, acting as if there were no neighbors nearby. They do not allow others to hear of the sins they have committed themselves;
instead, they proclaim their own anger to all. For this reason, there are clear witnesses that leave no room for concealment.
Just as a person’s every hair and pore is exposed when standing in the midday sun, there are the "Karma Mirror" and the "Fire Jewel" to reveal past karmic deeds and confront the individual with them.
"Examining such matters, we see that for this reason all Buddhas name them 'shadows and thieves' (*skandha-śatru*). 'Color' (*varṇa*) refers to concealment.
When Bodhisattvas observe this concealment, it is as if they were carrying a high mountain upon their heads while treading upon a vast ocean.

From beginningless time until this present life, I and the assembly have ultimately remained unaware of our habitual tendencies toward delusion, our attachment to false conditions, our hiding and protecting of flaws, and our harboring of faults. Once these [faults] are spoken of, there is no virtue."
They do not reform. When they speak ill of others, what evil will they not commit? Their temperament is arrogant and haughty; their eyes look down on everyone as if no one existed.
They cause disturbances both in public and private affairs, their speech being skillfully contrived. For years and even generations, there has been no end to this.

Furthermore, they give vent to private resentment and manifest their wicked forms, disregarding their own lives and bodies—how could they have any concern for their families? Their thoughts continue incessantly, their minds fixed solely upon others. Thus they dwell upon them...

Their thoughts are endless; they seek only their own gratification. Such causes and conditions all arise from restlessness (*auddhatya*), resulting in grave clamor that recurs in succession without a moment’s pause.

Therefore, today, in the presence of the World-Honored One and Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, I confess these ten habitual causes—from the habit of lust to the clamor of litigation—which produce hundreds of thousands of karmas and lead to the six realms of hell.
The retributions received through sensory contact, as well as the three miserable realms, all arise from this. I shall lay each and every one bare and repent again and again.

I pray that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will pour down the great nectar to drench and extinguish the causes of habitual tendencies; that the brilliant light of their wisdom-flame will incinerate the darkness of ignorance;
that my practices and vows may be fulfilled, my meditative contemplations profound, and the *prajñā-pāramitā* fully perfected; and that the Cloud of Dharma may pervade all realms, universally...
Sheltering all capacities, the rain of Dharma moistens and nourishes them. Together we clarify the seeds of the Way, cultivate the power of the Bodhisattva vows, and realize unsurpassed Bodhi.
Ultimately and perfectly accomplishing the wondrous practices of the Ten Stages, we join our hearts with sincere resolve and equal, piercing earnestness.
Prostrating ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground like the collapsing of Mount Tai, we take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas.
